extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students and instructors in algebraic topology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and results about cup product, the cohomology ring (graded ring structure and graded commutativity), the cross/external cup product, tensor-product algebra needed for a Künneth formula, and a number of concrete calculations (projective spaces, tori, James construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology ring via cup product
rubrics_metrics.description: Since cup product is associative and distributive, define H*(X; R) to be the direct sum of the groups H^n(X; R); elements are finite sums ∑_i α_i with α_i ∈ H^i(X; R), and the product of two such sums is defined componentwise by cup product (so ∑_i α_i · ∑_j β_j = ∑_{i,j} α_iβ_j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes H*(X; R) into a ring, with identity if R has an identity. Similarly H*(X,A;R) is a ring via relative cup product. Taking scalar multiplication into account, these rings are R-algebras. Example: H*(RP^2; Z_2) is Z_2[α]/(α^3). Adding different-dimensional classes into H* is a formal device; the meaningful structure is graded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graded ring structure (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A graded ring is a ring A with a decomposition as a sum ⊕_{k≥0} A_k of additive subgroups such that multiplication takes A_k × A_ℓ to A_{k+ℓ}. To indicate a ∈ A_k write |a| = k (called 'dimension' here).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies in particular to H^k(X;R). Some authors call |a| the 'degree' but the text uses 'dimension' to avoid confusion with polynomial degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graded commutativity (sign rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: In cohomology the commutativity property is ab = (−1)^{|a||b|} ba (Theorem 3.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In algebraic topology this is usually called 'commutative' (meaning graded commutative); older literature uses graded commutative / anticommutative / skew commutative. Consequence: to realize certain polynomial algebras as cohomology rings one must account for parity of generator dimensions or torsion in R (e.g., for RP^n one needs either |α| even or 2=0 in R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product / external cup product
rubrics_metrics.description: The cross product (external cup product) is the map H*(X;R) × H*(Y;R) → H*(X×Y;R) given by a × b = p_1^*(a) ∪ p_2^*(b) where p_1 and p_2 are projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cross product is bilinear (linear in each variable). Because bilinear maps induce homomorphisms from tensor products, the cross product gives rise to a homomorphism H*(X;R) ⊗_R H*(Y;R) → H*(X×Y;R). With the graded-tensor product multiplication sign convention (see next item) this map can be made a ring homomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product algebra facts used in Künneth
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic properties of tensor products for abelian groups and R-modules used: (1) A⊗B ≈ B⊗A, (2) (⊕_i A_i)⊗B ≈ ⊕_i (A_i⊗B), (3) (A⊗B)⊗C ≈ A⊗(B⊗C), (4) Z⊗A ≈ A, (5) Z_n ⊗ A ≈ A/nA, (6) pair of homomorphisms f⊗g induced, (7) bilinear map φ:A×B→C induces A⊗B→C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties guarantee the cross product factors through the tensor product and allow algebraic computations needed in Künneth arguments. Also generalize to R-modules by imposing r a⊗b = a⊗ r b so A⊗_R B becomes an R-module; statements (1),(2),(3),(6),(7) remain valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graded tensor-product multiplication sign convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Define multiplication in a tensor product of graded rings by (a⊗b)(c⊗d) = (−1)^{|b||c|} ac ⊗ bd where |x| denotes the dimension of x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With this sign convention the cross product map µ becomes a ring homomorphism: µ((a⊗b)(c⊗d)) = µ(a⊗b) µ(c⊗d). This sign twist is necessary to match graded commutativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Künneth isomorphism hypotheses (Theorem 3.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cross product H*(X;R) ⊗_R H*(Y;R) → H*(X×Y;R) is an isomorphism of rings if X and Y are CW complexes and H_k(Y;R) is a finitely generated free R-module for all k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CW hypothesis can be removed by CW approximations (discussed later); the freeness hypothesis cannot always be dispensed with (see §3.B for homology Künneth counterexamples). When the theorem applies, the ring structure of H*(X×Y;R) is determined by those of H*(X;R) and H*(Y;R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof strategy for Künneth via cohomology theories and naturality
rubrics_metrics.description: Define functors h_n(X,A)=⊕_i H^i(X,A;R)⊗_R H^{n−i}(Y;R) and k_n(X,A)=H^n(X×Y, A×Y;R) and show (1) h* and k* are cohomology theories on CW pairs and (2) µ is a natural transformation commuting with induced and coboundary maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the four axioms for unreduced cohomology (homotopy invariance, excision, long exact sequence of a pair, disjoint unions) for h* and use naturality and the five-lemma plus induction on CW skeleta (Prop 3.17: a natural transformation between unreduced cohomology theories that is an iso on the point is an iso for all CW pairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Künneth formula (Theorem 3.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: For CW pairs (X,A) and (Y,B) the cross product H*(X,A;R) ⊗_R H*(Y,B;R) → H*(X×Y, A×Y ∪ X×B; R) is an isomorphism of rings if H_k(Y,B;R) is a finitely generated free R-module for each k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to absolute case B=∅ by collapsing B to a point and applying five-lemma; further reductions use retraction and splitting arguments when B is a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced homomorphisms are ring homomorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Induced homomorphisms on cohomology (f^*: H*(X')→H*(X)) preserve cup product, i.e., are ring homomorphisms (Proposition 3.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: product rings: H*(⊔_α X_α;R) ≈ ∏_α H*(X_α;R) and inclusions induce coordinatewise ring homomorphisms; maps between spaces respect cup products by naturality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cup product to distinguish homotopy types
rubrics_metrics.description: Cup products can distinguish spaces that cannot be distinguished by additive cohomology groups alone (example: CP^2 is not homotopy equivalent to S^2 ∨ S^4 because the square of a generator of H^2(CP^2;Z) is nonzero, while squares are zero in H^*(S^2 ∨ S^4;Z)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cup product ring structure often yields more discriminating invariants than the sequence of groups H^n(X;R) viewed separately; this motivates the study of cohomology rings and invariants like the Hopf invariant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology rings of projective spaces (Theorem 3.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: H*(RP^n; Z_2) ≈ Z_2[α]/(α^{n+1}) and H*(RP^∞; Z_2) ≈ Z_2[α] with |α|=1. For complex projective spaces H*(CP^n; Z) ≈ Z[α]/(α^{n+1}) and H*(CP^∞; Z) ≈ Z[α] with |α|=2; quaternionic projective spaces give |α|=4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use geometry of projective spaces and Künneth / excision / cellular cohomology arguments; consequences include computations for RP^∞ with Z coefficients (H*(RP^∞;Z) ≈ Z[α]/(2α) with |α|=2) and formulas for finite RP^{2k}, RP^{2k+1} including torsion generators (see text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced cross product and suspension isomorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: For pointed spaces the relative cross product gives a reduced cross product H*(X;R) ⊗_R H*(Y;R) → H*(X ∧ Y;R). In particular, cross product with a generator of H^k(S^k;R) yields suspension isomorphisms H^n(X;R) ≈ H^{n+k}(X ∧ S^k;R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reduced cross product is an isomorphism if H*(Y;R) is finitely generated free in each degree (as in the absolute Künneth theorem). Useful for establishing suspension isomorphisms and computations involving smash products.

rubrics_metrics.name: James reduced product cohomology (Proposition 3.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: For J(S^n) the James reduced product, H*(J(S^n);Z) consists of a Z in each dimension a multiple of n. For n even the ith power of a generator of H^n(J(S^n);Z) is i! times a generator in degree i n; for n odd certain combinatorial relations hold (formulas given in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: for n even H*(J(S^n);Z) can be identified with the divided polynomial algebra (subring of Q[x] additively generated by x^i/i!). Over Q one recovers Q[x]; over Z_p one gets different structures described later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-ring matters for tensor products (caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ⊗_R B can differ from A ⊗ B when R ≠ Z (example: R = Z[√2] as a ring gives different ranks for R ⊗_R R vs R ⊗ R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When R = Z or Z_m or Q or any subring of Q one often has A ⊗_R B = A ⊗ B, but one must be careful for other base rings. This affects Künneth-type computations and freeness hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Realization Problem (which graded algebras occur as H*(X;R))
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: which graded commutative R-algebras occur as cup-product algebras H*(X;R) of spaces X?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of difficulty depends on coefficient ring R: R=Q is most accessible (essentially every graded commutative Q-algebra is realizable, per Quillen 1969), R=Z_p is much harder with only partial results known, and R=Z is hardest with little known beyond implications from the Z_p cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain-homotopy via prism operator (construction guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a chain homotopy between ρ and the identity, construct a prism operator P: C_n(X) → C_{n+1}(X) (motivated by subdivision of Δ^n × I into (n+1) simplices) so that ∂P + P∂ = ρ − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses a specific ordering of vertices (v_0,...,v_n,w_n,...,w_0) and sign conventions ε_{n−i}; verify cancellations in boundary computations to obtain ∂P + P∂ = ρ − 1. The same construction applies relative to a subcomplex A since ρ and P take chains in A to chains in A, and dual homomorphisms act on relative cochains.
